title: AB de Villiers Declares Kohli Better Than Tendulkar in Tests, Sparks Fresh Debate
excerpt: The former South African captain has gone further than his previous balanced take, asserting Kohli was stronger than Tendulkar in Test cricket — a claim that has drawn immediate pushback from analysts and fans.
body:
• AB de Villiers has reignited the Kohli-Tendulkar debate by asserting that Virat Kohli was the better Test batter, calling him stronger than Sachin Tendulkar in the format
  • The comments mark a shift from de Villiers' earlier balanced stance, where he described Kohli as an "all-format great" and Tendulkar as a "longer format" master
  • Former India player Cheteshwar Pujara and the Hindustan Times have pushed back, arguing Tendulkar's overseas Test record was superior to Kohli's

De Villiers Tips the Scale Toward Kohli

AB de Villiers has made his boldest intervention yet in cricket's most debated comparison, declaring that Virat Kohli was the better Test batter when measured against Sachin Tendulkar. The former South African captain, who played 114 Tests and scored 8,756 runs at an average above 50, said Tendulkar was "not as strong" as Kohli in the five-day format, according to multiple reports including The Times of India and News18.

The comments have set off a firestorm among cricket fans, particularly in India where the Kohli-Tendulkar comparison remains one of the sport's most charged conversations.

De Villiers, who played against both batsmen during his international career spanning 2004 to 2018, has long walked a careful line on the topic. In a 2025 podcast with Shubhankar Mishra during the World Championship of Legends, he had offered a more diplomatic assessment.

"You can't compare different generations. I have lots of respect for Sachin, looked up to him. Virat is more my friend. I think Virat was an all-format great, Sachin in longer format."

— AB de Villiers, in a 2025 podcast interview

His latest comments, however, go further — positioning Kohli not just as an all-format great but as the superior Test batter outright.

The Numbers Behind the Debate

Kohli retired from Test cricket in early 2025 with 9,230 runs at an average of nearly 47, including 30 centuries in 113 matches. His peak years between 2016 and 2019 saw him reach a career-high ICC ranking of 900 points — a mark that even Tendulkar never achieved, though Tendulkar peaked at 898.

Tendulkar's Test record, accumulated over 200 matches and 24 years, stands at 15,921 runs at an average of 53.78 with 51 centuries. He remains the only batter with 100 international centuries across all formats.

The raw numbers favor Tendulkar in volume and consistency. But de Villiers' argument appears to center on intensity and physical dominance — the "strength" he referenced in describing Kohli's approach to Test cricket.

Pushback From Analysts and Former Players

The claim has not gone unchallenged. The Hindustan Times published an analysis arguing that de Villiers "gets his research wrong," noting that Tendulkar's overseas Test batting record — often the truest measure of a Test batter's quality — was demonstrably superior to Kohli's.

NDTV reported that former India batter Cheteshwar Pujara also expressed his views following the Galle Test, though his comments focused on broader bowling analysis rather than the comparison directly.

Former South African pacer Allan Donald had earlier offered a more nuanced take, saying in January 2026: "If there's one batter who is going to get close to Sachin Tendulkar, it would be Virat Kohli. I don't think I've ever seen a hunger in a player like Virat."

Why the Debate Endures

The Kohli-Tendulkar comparison refuses to settle because it pits two fundamentally different eras against each other. Tendulkar played his first Test in 1989, when pitches were uncovered, helmets were rudimentary, and batsmen faced undiluted pace attacks over five-day Tests scheduled weeks apart. Kohli's career unfolded in an era of packed schedules, data-driven bowling strategies, and the Decision Review System.

De Villiers is one of the few active voices who shared a dressing room with Kohli at Royal Challengers Bengaluru in the IPL (2011-2021) and faced Tendulkar in international cricket. That dual perspective gives his opinions unusual weight, even when they provoke disagreement.

For cricket-obsessed diaspora fans — who grew up watching Tendulkar on grainy television feeds and followed Kohli's career in real-time on streaming platforms — the debate is less about statistics and more about generational identity. De Villiers' latest comments ensure it will rage on.
